NEW DELHI: India and Nepal on Monday signed eight agreements to expand cooperation in sectors including space technology, security, healthcare, agriculture and sustainable urban development, following talks between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah in New Delhi.The two leaders also virtually flagged off the Saryu-Kamala Express, connecting Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh with Janakpur in Nepal, and jointly inaugurated several development projects during Balen Shah’s two-day state visit to India.At a joint press conference after the talks, Modi said the two countries had taken several important decisions to strengthen bilateral relations.“I am very pleased to welcome Balendra Shah ji to India on his first bilateral visit after becoming the Prime Minister of Nepal. A few months ago, when he addressed the United Nations as the world’s youngest Prime Minister, we got a clear glimpse of his vision. Over the past few hours of our discussions, I have sensed his clear vision and commitment towards Nepal’s future and India-Nepal relations. The historic mandate given to him by the people of Nepal this year reflects the aspirations and hopes of the country’s younger generation. India has always been a partner in the development journey of a strong and prosperous Nepal.In this spirit, today we have taken several important decisions to take our relations to new heights,” PM Modi said.The prime minister also announced a development cooperation package of 24,000 crore Nepali rupees (approximately Rs 15,000 crore) to support Nepal’s reconstruction and long-term development, particularly in the wake of the devastating floods in August.“We express our deep condolences for the loss of lives caused by the devastating floods in Nepal in August. Today, we announce a development cooperation package of 24,000 crore Nepali rupees to give fresh impetus to Nepal’s reconstruction and long-term development. Our commitment will be to help affected families get their lives back on track, create new opportunities, and further strengthen Nepal’s capacity to deal with future disasters,” he said.PM Modi also highlighted the shared religious and cultural ties between the two countries, referring to the launch of the train service connecting Ayodhya and Janakpur.“Lord Ram and Mata Sita are symbols of our shared civilisation and faith. In 2018, on the sacred land of Janakpur, I had said that our pilgrimage sites are incomplete without Nepal, and our Lord Ram is incomplete without Nepal. In 2024, the consecration ceremony of Ram Lalla took place in Ayodhya. This historic occasion gave renewed strength to our shared faith…With the launch of the Sarayu-Kamala Express train service today, we are giving a new dimension to this sacred bond,” he said.He said India had maintained supplies of fuel and other essential goods to Nepal despite serious challenges related to oil supplies this year, and expressed confidence in the future of bilateral ties.“We will together write a golden chapter of India-Nepal relations,” PM Modi said.The Saryu-Kamala Express will connect Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh with Janakpur Dham in Nepal, covering around 604 km in approximately 19 hours. The regular service will operate once a week in each direction from November 28, enabling pilgrims to travel between the two religious destinations without changing trains.The inaugural run on Monday operated as a special train (No. 04295), departing from Ayodhya Dham at 12.30 pm.The eight MoUs exchanged after the delegation-level talks cover satellite communication, policing, forensic sciences, civil service training, healthcare, traditional medicine, sustainable urban development, and livestock and fisheries development.In the space and communication sector, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and Nepal’s Ministry of Information and Communication signed an MoU to establish a Satellite Communication (SATCOM) Network for the utilisation of the South Asia Satellite.Two agreements aim to strengthen cooperation in policing and forensic sciences. One provides for academic and research collaboration between the National Forensic Sciences University in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, and the Crime Investigation Department of Nepal Police. The other was signed between India’s Rashtriya Raksha University and Nepal’s National Police Academy.For capacity building in public administration, the National Centre for Good Governance, under India’s Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, signed an MoU with Nepal’s Administrative Staff College under the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration. The agreement provides for training programmes for Nepalese civil servants.In healthcare, India’s Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and Nepal’s Ministry of Health and Food Safety signed an MoU on cooperation in health and medicine. The two sides also signed a government-to-government agreement on cooperation in Ayurveda and other traditional systems of medicine.The remaining two agreements provide for technical cooperation in sustainable urban development and collaboration in livestock and fisheries development.At the joint press conference, Balen Shah described India-Nepal relations as being founded on mutual respect, trust and goodwill.“Ties between India and Nepal stand as firm as the Himalayas and as vast as oceans,” he said.He expressed confidence that the agreements and initiatives announced during the visit would take bilateral relations to a new level, while stressing the need for cooperation on climate change.“I am confident that these historic milestones will elevate Nepal-India relations to new heights. The need of the hour is to build on the strong foundation of this enduring relationship and lay solid pillars for the future. Our Himalayas, the sources of clean water, sustain millions across this region. The pristine rivers flowing from the Himalayas into the Ganga remind us of our future and destiny, underscoring the need to address the challenges of climate change through collective action. Nepal and India have been bound by historical, cultural and civilisational ties since the sacred era of Lord Ram and Mata Janaki,” Balen Shah said.Balen Shah arrived in New Delhi on Sunday for a two-day state visit, his first to India since assuming office in March 2026.On Monday, PM Modi received him at Hyderabad House for the bilateral talks. Before the meeting, Shah was accorded a ceremonial welcome at Rashtrapati Bhavan and paid floral tributes to Mahatma Gandhi at the Raj Ghat memorial.Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in a post on X that the leaders would discuss various aspects of bilateral relations and explore new avenues to deepen cooperation.Jaiswal described the ceremonial welcome as reflecting “the special warmth and enduring friendship between India and Nepal” and Shah’s visit to Raj Ghat as “A tribute to the timeless legacy of Mahatma!”
Article Summary: India and Nepal signed eight agreements to expand cooperation in sectors including space technology, security, healthcare, agriculture and sustainable urban development. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah virtually flagged off the Saryu-Kamala Express, connecting Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh with Janakpur in Nepal.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday suspended the sentence of Irfan Siraj Pada, a convict in the 2002 Godhra train burning case , and granted him bail on medical grounds, taking note of his serious cardiovascular condition and more than 17 years in custody.A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale passed the order after considering his medical condition, which the Gujarat government did not dispute, LiveLaw reported on Monday.According to legal news portal, the court took into account that Irfan suffers from a serious cardiovascular disease and has remained incarcerated for over 17 years. His appeal against the conviction is pending before the Supreme Court.The Godhra train burning took place on February 27, 2002, when 58 people were killed in a fire inside the S-6 coach of the Sabarmati Express, which was carrying kar sevaks returning from Ayodhya. The incident triggered communal riots across Gujarat.In March 2011, a trial court convicted 31 people in the case. Eleven were sentenced to death, while the remaining 20 were awarded life imprisonment. In 2017, the Gujarat high court commuted the death sentences of the 11 convicts to life terms and upheld the life sentences awarded to the other 20.Appeals against the convictions have been pending before the Supreme Court since 2018, LiveLaw reported.Irfan had also been granted interim parole in 2025 to allow the state government to consider his plea for premature release, according to the report.The latest order comes days after the Supreme Court suspended the life sentences of two other convicts in a separate case linked to the 2002 Gujarat riots . Last Tuesday, the court granted bail to Bipin Chandra Joshi and Pradeep Mordhiya, who were convicted in the gangrape of Bilkis Bano and the murder of seven members of her family.In an order dated October 28, uploaded subsequently, a bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale noted that the two men had spent more than 17 years in prison and that one of them had a severe disability.“Having heard the parties, suffice it to state that the appellants have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years, and also the fact remains that one of the appellants has a severe handicap. Certainly, there are issues to be decided in the appeal, both on fact and law,” the bench said.“In view of the above and considering the issues involved in this appeal, we suspend the sentence and grant bail to the appellants on such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the concerned trial court,” it added.
Article Summary: Supreme Court grants medical bail to convict after 17 years in jail. 58 people were killed in a fire inside the S-6 coach of the Sabarmati Express, which was carrying kar sevaks returning from Ayodhya. In March 2011, a trial court convicted 31 people in the case.

Article Title: Half a course, full consequences: How India is losing its antibiotics
Article Text:
How India is losing its antibiotics

A problem that has moved into the clinic

What hospital laboratories are finding

Why

antibiotics

are prescribed when they may not be needed

The half-finished course

When the first drug fails

What the rules say

What the government is attempting

A caution about the numbers

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What one doctor would change

Most Indian households know the routine. A fever lingers, a half-used strip of tablets from an earlier illness sits in the drawer, and the corner chemist asks few questions. Two doses later the fever eases and the strip goes back into the drawer. It feels like a small, sensible saving.Inside the body, the picture is different. The bacteria that survive a partial course are often the hardiest ones, and they are left free to multiply. Multiplied across millions of households, hospitals, pharmacies and farms, this is how a medicine stops working.Antimicrobial resistance occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive medicines that once killed them. An infection that a common antibiotic could treat becomes harder to control, pushing doctors toward stronger, costlier drugs.Doctors say they see this daily. Dr Sowmya Muralikumaran, an internal medicine specialist at Apollo Spectra hospital in Chennai, is asked how often she now sees infections that do not respond to the first antibiotic prescribed."Very often," she says, "especially with patients who have self-medicated with multiple medicines before coming for a consultation."The national picture is documented in the annual report of the Indian Council of Medical Research's (ICMR) Antimicrobial Resistance Research and Surveillance Network, which for 2025 analysed 1,13,008 culture-positive bacterial and fungal samples from 30 tertiary-care hospitals. For the first time, it also included data from 34 secondary-care hospitals, 12 of them district hospitals, which contributed another 20,529 samples.The findings are stark. Only 18.4 per cent of E. coli samples responded to cefotaxime and 24.7 per cent to ceftazidime. Among E. coli from urine samples, just 9 per cent were sensitive to ciprofloxacin and 18.2 per cent to levofloxacin. Low sensitivity was seen even among patients visiting outpatient departments, which suggests resistance is not confined to those admitted to hospital.Klebsiella pneumoniae, which can cause bloodstream and lung infections, fared worse. Sensitivity to third-generation cephalosporins was between 23 and 27 per cent. Carbapenems, powerful drugs that doctors turn to when others fail, worked against only 35 to 40 per cent of samples. The report found genes such as OXA-48 and NDM, which help bacteria survive carbapenems, in some Klebsiella samples.Intensive care units showed the heaviest burden. Sensitivity of ICU Klebsiella samples to ertapenem, imipenem and meropenem was 26.1, 24.9 and 26.3 per cent, respectively. Among Acinetobacter baumannii samples that were retested, 91.1 per cent were resistant to carbapenems. More than half of Staphylococcus aureus samples (56.8 per cent) from tertiary hospitals were methicillin-resistant, or MRSA, and about one in five enterococci samples was resistant to vancomycin.Typhoid shows how uneven the picture can be. Samples remained highly sensitive to azithromycin (99.4 per cent) and ceftriaxone (96.6 per cent), but only 2 per cent responded to ciprofloxacin.There is some good news. Fosfomycin worked against 96.5 per cent of urine E. coli samples and nitrofurantoin against 79.1 per cent. The report is clear that these are laboratory findings, and the right drug still depends on the site and severity of infection and on the patient's own tests.Doctors do not always prescribe antibiotics because patients demand them, but expectations play a part. Dr Muralikumaran points to two reasons."Many people have this feeling that only when they take antibiotics will they heal," she says. The second reason lies with the doctor. "There is uncertainty in diagnosis. Mostly all of us might have a viral infection, but sometimes it might be bacterial, so in fear of missing a bacterial infection, an antibiotic can be prescribed too."Antibiotics do not act on viruses. Yet a viral and a bacterial illness can look alike in the first days, and without a quick, affordable test the cautious choice is often to prescribe.The patient's side of the story begins before the consultation. "Quite many have already taken antibiotics," Dr Muralikumaran says. "What they usually do is, after one or two doses, they will feel fine and drop it. They will not fully finish their course."Self-medication then complicates what comes next. A patient who arrives after taking several medicines at home presents a doctor with a muddier clinical picture and, possibly, a more resistant infection.Once an antibiotic fails, she says, swapping it for another is not enough. "Simply recommending an antibiotic will not help." The patient has to be reassessed: symptoms re-examined, more detailed blood tests ordered, and only then a higher antibiotic prescribed, sometimes by a different route.The ICMR report makes a similar point. It highlights that identifying the specific resistance mechanism can help doctors decide which newer medicines may work, and it advises choosing antibiotics based on laboratory testing rather than on what worked in the past.The cost falls on the patient. "It does have a cost on their finances," Dr Muralikumaran says, "and their recovery time also might get delayed."On paper, India restricts how antibiotics are sold. They are listed under Schedules H and H1 of the Drugs Rules, 1945, which means a registered medical practitioner's prescription is needed. Schedule H1, in force since 2014, adds stricter conditions: pharmacies must record each sale in a separate register, and under the rules, these supply records are to be kept for three years.The health ministry's Red Line campaign asks the public not to use medicines marked with a red vertical line, including antibiotics, without a doctor's prescription.Enforcement is another matter. Studies of retail practice have found that over-the-counter sale of antibiotics remains widespread despite these measures. A 2019 study in Kerala that interviewed pharmacy owners found a general perception that the regulations were poorly enforced, and that awareness of the Red Line campaign was patchy, even among healthcare professionals.India's policy effort stretches back more than a decade. The country formed a National Task Force on AMR Containment in 2010 and published its first National Action Plan on AMR in 2017. The second, NAP-AMR 2.0 for 2025 to 2029, was launched by Union Health Minister J P Nadda on 18 November 2025, the first day of the World Health Organization's World AMR Awareness Week.At the launch, Nadda said the misuse and overuse of antibiotics had become an unfortunate common practice. The health ministry said the new plan addresses gaps in the first by increasing ownership of AMR efforts, improving coordination between sectors and engaging more closely with the private sector. It follows a One Health approach, which treats human, animal and environmental health together.Some states have moved on their own. Kerala was the first state to introduce a state action plan on AMR, in 2018. In January 2024, its Drug Control Department launched Operation AMRITH, which involves surprise inspections of pharmacies to detect sales of antibiotics without a prescription. Pharmacies must display a notice saying antibiotics will not be sold without one and must keep accurate sales records. Citizens can report violations on a toll-free number.The ICMR figures come from hospital laboratories, largely tertiary-care centres, and they show how many samples responded to a drug in testing. They do not show how many patients failed treatment, developed complications or died. They also do not reflect resistance levels in the wider community. Even so, the direction they point in is clear, and ICMR itself has called for better antibiotic use, stronger infection control in hospitals and treatment guided by local resistance patterns.Asked what single change she would make, Dr Muralikumaran does not hesitate."We should start prescribing antibiotics only after establishing a bacterial disease," she says, "and pharmacies should start giving antibiotics based on a prescription."It is a modest-sounding request. It asks doctors to wait for a diagnosis, patients to finish the course they are given, and chemists to ask for the slip of paper. Each of those habits is small, and the damage from skipping them adds up across the country.
Article Summary: Antimicrobial resistance occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive medicines that once killed them. An infection that a common antibiotic could treat becomes harder to control, pushing doctors toward stronger, costlier drugs. The report is clear that these are laboratory findings, and the right drug still has to be found.

NEW DELHI: Congress general secretary and Punjab in-charge Sachin Pilot on Monday termed the reported possibility of a renewed alliance between the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) in Punjab as “pure opportunism”, questioning what had changed since the two parties parted ways.He also criticised the Bhagwant Mann-led Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) government and said Congress could provide an alternative ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections.Addressing the media in Amritsar, Pilot questioned whether the issues that led to the BJP and Akali Dal ending their alliance had been resolved.“Look, the Bharatiya Janata Party has said all those things against the Akali Dal when their mutual agreement ended and for what reasons the alliance between the Akali Dal and BJP had broken. So many people lost their lives in the protest. The Akali Dal and the BJP should answer why they are together today. NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah arrived at Hyderabad House in New Delhi on Monday for bilateral talks aimed at reviewing ties between the two countries and exploring ways to expand cooperation across key sectors.The discussions are expected to cover the full range of India-Nepal relations, including economic cooperation, trade, investment, transportation, infrastructure, energy and connectivity, as well as regional and international developments of mutual interest.According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), the November 22-23 visit is being held at the invitation of Prime Minister Modi. Announcing the visit, the Ministry said the two leaders would review bilateral relations and exchange views on regional and international issues."Prime Minister Modi will hold bilateral talks with Prime Minister of Nepal on 23 November 2026 to review the full range of India–Nepal relations and exchange views on regional and international issues of mutual interest," the Ministry stated.The MEA also underlined the historical, cultural and civilisational ties between the two countries, along with their strong people-to-people connections. It noted that bilateral cooperation had expanded across traditional sectors as well as newer areas such as start-ups, technology, innovation and sports."India and Nepal share close and friendly relations, rooted in historical, cultural and civilisational links and strong people-to-people ties. Bilateral cooperation has witnessed progress across diverse sectors, including trade and commerce, development partnership, energy and water resources, and physical and digital connectivity, with growing engagement in newer areas such as start-ups, technology and innovation, and sports," the Ministry said.Economic cooperation is expected to feature prominently in the discussions, with both sides looking to strengthen engagement in trade, transportation, investment and infrastructure development.The two countries are also expected to exchange memorandums of understanding (MoUs) in areas of mutual interest, including education, health, agriculture, sports, disaster management and human resource development.Connectivity and energy cooperation are among the other key areas on the agenda. The two sides are expected to inaugurate completed projects in these sectors and lay foundation stones for new initiatives.The visit will also include a Nepal-India Business Forum, which is aimed at attracting Indian investment to Nepal and providing business representatives from both countries an opportunity to explore partnerships and strengthen commercial ties.Modi will host an official luncheon for Shah and his 34-member delegation.Earlier in the day, Balen Shah paid tribute to Mahatma Gandhi at his memorial in Raj Ghat, where he laid a wreath and signed the visitors' book.Before this, the Nepalese Prime Minister received a ceremonial Guard of Honour at Rashtrapati Bhavan in the presence of Modi.Balen Shah is accompanied by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal, Chief Advisor to the Prime Minister Kumar Byanjankar and other senior government officials.The two-day state visit provides an opportunity for both countries to review ongoing cooperation and discuss ways to strengthen their bilateral partnership across areas of shared interest.

After police pick up a person, they have exactly 24 hours to produce them before a magistrate. SC has made it clear the deadline starts at the point of detention — not when the arrest is recorded — and exceeding it amounts to a violation of fundamental rights.explains. Supreme Court 's order on detention without prompt production before a magistrate speaks to one of the most fundamental rights - the right to freedom of movement. This is significant because this deadline has often been violated by delay in recording an arrest.The top court has clarified that only the time needed to travel from the place of arrest to the magistrate's court to produce a suspect can be excluded from the timeframe. Time spent in questioning, searches, seizures or other legal formalities must count towards the deadline.The court, in fact, also went a step further and clarified that sticking to the 24-hour window does not automatically make detention reasonable.In plain English, a suspect must not be held in custody unnecessarily just because police have 24 hours to produce him before a magistrate. They must justify every hour of curtailment of a suspect's freedom of movement and magistrates must examine how long a person was held and whether that period was justified.The Nov 5 order followed appeals by three men accused in a case involving the alleged transportation of over 60kg of contraband drugs in Tripura. A bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar held that their detention violated Art 22(2) of the Constitution and Sec 58 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 and set aside Tripura High Court's order rejecting their bail pleas.Customs officials had taken the men into custody on Sept 29, 2025 and their arrests were formally recorded the next morning. They were produced before a magistrate more than 24 hours after they were first detained (see box).Art 22(2) of the Constitution says an arrested person has to be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours. Detention beyond 24 hours requires a magistrate's authority. SC said the clock starts when a suspect is detained and their freedom is restricted, that is, "when his liberty is effectively curtailed".There is no constitutional basis, it said, for excluding time spent on investigation, interrogation, or legal formalities from the mandated 24 hours.The court also referred to Sec 58 of BNSS, which reflects the restriction in Sec 57 of the earlier Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), requiring detention to last no longer than is reasonable in the circumstances, even within the 24-hour limit.Additional solicitor general Raghavendra P Shankar, representing the Union govt, said the intervening hours before they were produced before a magistrate had been taken up by mandatory procedures like searches, seizures, preparing documents, questioning the accused, etc. He argued that arrest memos could be prepared only after the initial investigation. Until then, they were temporarily restrained to allow the search and seizure process to be completed.The govt relied on Rule 3(4) of NDPS Rules, 2022, which requires seized substances to be classified, weighed, packaged and numbered in the presence of search witnesses and the person from whom they were recovered. The govt argued that the time taken for these necessary steps could not be treated as detention following arrest.The bench examined earlier judgments on what amounts to arrest and custody, including a March 1980 SC judgment that held a person is in custody as soon as he is under the control of an investigating agency or an authority with powers to restrain him. Apart from citing these judgments in support of the accused, SC also rejected three HC decisions relied on by the govt, including Kannan vs State of Tamil Nadu (2026) that held that time spent on mandatory NDPS procedures before formal arrest could be excluded from the 24-hour calculation.SC instead said that search and seizure procedures did not prevent timely production before a magistrate. They could continue after production and authorisation of judicial custody.The judgment linked prompt production before a magistrate to protection against custodial violence. It cited a Dec 1980 SC judgment - against the backdrop of the Bhagalpur blinding incidents involving prisoners - that said the 24-hour requirement allowed judicial authorities to keep a check on police investigations.The bench also referred to the D K Basu case - that highlighted custodial violence and the practice of questioning suspects without formally recording their arrests, in which SC issued arrest safeguards in mid-90s. The latest judgment recalled earlier judicial concerns about people arrested without warrants being tortured to extract information, recover property or obtain confessions. It also cited an SC ruling in an Enforcement Directorate case, which held that a breach of Art 22(2) makes an arrest invalid and requires the court hearing the bail plea to release the accused.The court also examined Sec 37 of NDPS Act, which sets strict conditions for bail in cases involving commercial quantities of drugs. Tripura High Court had relied on an April 2026 ruling by a two-judge SC bench that held the two conditions under Sec 37 must be met before bail could be granted in such cases.The latest Supreme Court ruling questioned the suggestion that the right to a speedy trial under Art 21 must operate within the framework of Sec 37. It relied on the landmark Feb 2021 decision in Union of India vs KA Najeeb, where a three-judge SC bench recognised that strict provisions in special laws could not override fundamental rights under Art 21. It also made clear that NDPS procedures could not weaken the protection against unlawful detention under Art 22(2). In this case, the court found that the unexplained 18-hour gap between the end of search and seizure and the formal arrests was unreasonable under Sec 58 of BNSS, which states that "no police officer shall detain a person arrested without a warrant in custody for longer than is reasonable under the circumstances".
Article Summary: Art 22(2) of the Constitution says an arrested person has to be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours. The deadline has often been violated by delay in recording an arrest. Time spent in questioning, searches, seizures or other legal formalities must count towards the deadline.
